rationale: All 6 candidates are direct matches (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate abdominal aortic aneurysm). PGS000753 is best supported because it is disease-focused (Million Veteran Program AAA paper), uses basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), and—critically—reports a PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.37, 95% CI 1.30–1.44), which is a PRS-comparable signal when many others mainly report full-model discrimination. As runners-up, PGS003973 (same AAA GWAS meta-analysis paper family) has strong study context and basic covariates (Age, Age^2, Sex) with a high reported C-index (0.882), but this appears to be a full-model metric (no PGS-only AUC/R2/effect size shown), limiting comparability. PGS002054 is a UKB portability-framework score (explicitly a portability paper) with only partial-r=0.0144 and no PRS-only AUC/OR, so it is weaker than disease-focused options but still provides a PRS-comparable metric. Overall confidence is moderate because key PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUC/OR/HR) are missing for most candidates, and several reported AUROCs/C-indices are likely full-model and thus not directly comparable for PRS ranking. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All 4 candidates are direct-match on concept for the target (alcohol dependence): PGS002738/PGS002739 have trait_efo="alcohol dependence" and phenotyping_reported="Alcohol use disorder"; PGS000201/PGS000202 are mapped to "alcohol dependence measurement" with phenotyping_reported="Alcohol use disorder (DSM-5 criteria count, log-transformed)", which is closely aligned but framed as a quantitative DSM-5 criteria count.

PGS002738 is best supported because it has the most directly disease-labeled endpoint (AUD) with trait_efo exactly matching alcohol dependence, and it reports a strong discriminative effect size (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.96, 95% CI 1.54–2.51) in European evaluation (n=7,900). This provides clearer PRS-relevant evidence than the UKB-only DSM-5 criteria-count models that report only small ΔR² values.

Runners-up: PGS002739 is also endpoint-faithful (AUD; trait_efo alcohol dependence) and reports a reasonably strong OR top 10% vs rest = 1.76 (1.32–2.34), but it is evaluated only in African American/Afro-Caribbean samples (EVAL: AFR 100%), making it less generally supported than the EUR-evaluated PGS002738 given the context does not specify a target ancestry. Among the remaining two, PGS000201 is preferred over PGS000202 because it shows stronger incremental variance explained (ΔR² 0.01192 vs 0.00456) and a larger beta (0.099 vs 0.043) in European evaluation, with similar phenotype framing.

Overall outcome is DIRECT_SUB_OPTIMAL (not high-quality) because none of the candidates report PRS-only AUROC or PRS-only R², covariates are unknown for PGS002738/PGS002739, and the two UKB-derived models show relatively small ΔR²; these limitations prevent a clearly definitive best choice despite PGS002738 being the most supported within the visible set.

All three candidates are direct matches to the target trait (trait_efo = alcoholic liver cirrhosis) with endpoint-faithful phenotyping labels. PGS004913 is preferred because it is explicitly designed for alcohol-associated cirrhosis among heavy drinkers (phenotyping_reported matches the target wording closely) and reports a PRS-comparable metric (R²=0.029) plus an OR top vs bottom PRS deciles of 4.4, with basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), making its evidence more directly interpretable as PRS signal than models reporting only full-model discrimination. Runner-up PGS001777 is also disease-focused and reports strong stratification (OR top 20% vs bottom 20% = 6.18) and AUROC=0.671, but it is a very sparse 3-variant score with unknown covariates and a small validation sample (n=1,390), which limits confidence. Runner-up PGS000704 has very large development/validation and a modern high-variant method (snpnet, 183k variants), but its only visible discrimination is a full-model C-index/AUC=0.711 (not explicitly PGS-only) and it comes from a broad biomarker genetics paper, so the PRS-specific contribution is unclear. Overall confidence is moderate because none of the candidates provides clearly comparable PGS-only AUROC, and two rely on full-model metrics or non-comparable effect-size summaries.

All 19 candidates are direct matches to angina pectoris by trait_efo and phenotyping_reported (Angina / ICD10 I20 / PheCode 411.3), so a direct-match exists. Among models with comparable reported discrimination, the MVP PheCode 411.3 set (PGS005047–PGS005059) provides consistent European evaluation C-index values (~0.75–0.77) and several report strong per-SD ORs (~1.45–1.49). PGS005052 is selected because it combines one of the highest reported European C-index values (0.766245) with a strong OR per SD (1.491, 95% CI 1.42–1.57), giving the best-supported PRS signal among the visible candidates. Runners-up are PGS005048 (slightly higher C-index 0.766876 but similar strong OR 1.487) and PGS005057 (C-index 0.766367 with OR 1.479), which remain very close on the same endpoint and evaluation context. Confidence is moderated because these MVP metrics are full-model C-index (not explicitly PGS-only), training sample size is listed as N/A, and several UKB-based alternatives either lack PRS-only metrics (e.g., PGS000703) or come from a pan-trait sparse framework (PGS001260–PGS001262) where high full-model AUROC is likely covariate-driven and less reliable for PRS ranking. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All 9 candidates are direct matches to the target trait (trait_efo = ankylosing spondylitis). PGS001267 is best supported because it has clear endpoint alignment (phenotyping_reported: Ankylosing spondylitis), reports PRS-comparable metrics including PGS-only AUROC (0.7265) and PGS-only R2 (0.0988), and uses only basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs). Its PRS-only R2 is also plausibly below the provided liability-scale heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.399), supporting metric sanity. Main limitation: it is from a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse framework paper ("across 813 traits"), which domain guidance flags as often less externally robust than disease-focused scores, and there is meaningful competition from other direct-match models.

Runner-up 1 (PGS001268): same study family, same basic covariates and PRS-only metrics, with slightly higher reported AUROC/R2 than PGS001267, but it is explicitly time-to-event (phenotyping_reported: TTE ankylosing spondylitis), which is a mild endpoint mismatch for a generic disease-risk target and lowers preference versus the non-TTE endpoint.

Runner-up 2 (PGS002089): direct ankylosing spondylitis endpoint with a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) and large variant count (22,026), which is structurally favorable; however, it comes from a UKB portability framework paper and lacks PRS-comparable AUROC/R2 (only partial correlation reported), making its performance evidence less directly comparable than PGS001267/PGS001268. The Taiwanese EAS-only models (PGS003420–PGS003424) report only full-model AUROC with unknown covariates and small validation (n=1,298), so their apparent AUROC advantage is not PRS-comparable and is weaker evidence for general direct-match selection here.

Direct-match candidates for aortic stenosis are present (PGS005252, PGS005254) plus closely aligned aortic valve function measures with aortic stenosis EFO and incident AS phenotyping (PGS005255/PGS005256). PGS005252 is best supported because it is an exact trait match (trait_reported/trait_efo = aortic stenosis) with endpoint-fidelity phenotyping (incident aortic stenosis cases), a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDPred2) with large variant count (~1.12M), and it reports a strong time-to-event discrimination metric (C-index 0.87) alongside HR=1.92; although the C-index is a full-model metric with multiple clinical covariates, the covariates are standard epidemiologic risk factors rather than explicit risk-calculator packaging. Runner-up PGS005254 is also an exact aortic stenosis model with incident AS phenotyping and a strong HR=1.64 (CI provided) using PRS-CS, but it lacks comparable discrimination metrics (no AUC/C-index/R2 shown) and has less explicit study/cohort detail in the visible fields. For the second runner-up, PGS005255 is selected over PGS005256 because both are near-identical aortic stenosis–anchored valve-function scores (same publication family, similar HR=1.53 with CIs, similar covariates and validation size), making them effectively indistinguishable; choosing one reflects that these are not exact ‘aortic stenosis’ trait_reported endpoints even though phenotyping_reported is incident AS. Confidence is Moderate because none of the direct AS candidates report PRS-only (covariate-free) AUC/R2, so cross-model performance comparability is limited and the high C-index for PGS005252 may be partly covariate-driven per the provided domain guidance. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

Direct-match candidates for the target trait (arthritis) are present, including an exact EFO match: PGS001135 ("Arthritis (nos)", trait_efo="arthritis", phenotyping_reported="Arthritis (nos)"). This provides the strongest endpoint/phenotype alignment to the generic target "arthritis" among the visible list. However, its PRS-only performance is weak (PGS AUROC (no covariates)=0.53928; PGS R2 (no covariates)=0.00291; incremental AUROC=0.00314), and the model comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank framework paper ("Significant sparse polygenic risk scores across 813 traits in UK Biobank"), which domain guidance flags as tending to generalize poorly versus disease-focused models—lowering confidence despite exact label match.

Runners-up are the other exact-EFO arthritis models visible: PGS004477 and PGS004547 (both "M13 (Other arthritis)", trait_efo="arthritis"), which are also direct matches but have limited comparable performance evidence (only an OR reported: ~1.20 for PGS004477 and ~1.26 for PGS004547; no AUROC/PRS-only R2 shown) and come from a risk-factor/PRS integration context (Commun Biol), making their standalone PRS strength harder to assess from the provided metadata. They remain the best-supported alternatives because other listed models (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, gout, juvenile idiopathic arthritis) are not direct matches to generic "arthritis". | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

Direct-match candidates are abundant (all map to asthma/asthma-related endpoints). PGS002727 is best supported because it is explicitly phenotype-aligned to a clinically relevant restricted form ("Pediatric asthma"), is disease-focused ("Multiancestral polygenic risk score for pediatric asthma"), shows moderate-to-strong PRS signal via effect size (OR=1.57 per SD) and reports full-model AUROC=0.66 with very large validation (n=391,820) across multi-ancestry evaluation; covariates are listed as unknown (a limitation, but not an explicit heavy-leakage covariate set). Runner-up PGS001344 has strong, cleanly reported PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.64568; PGS-only R2=0.05973) and strong full-model AUROC=0.66621, but it comes from a pan-trait UKB framework paper ("across 813 traits"), which domain guidance penalizes versus disease-focused models when a strong disease-focused option exists. Second runner-up PGS002061 (LDpred2, UKB portability framework) has supportive partial correlation (0.1184) and large training (UKB), but lacks directly comparable PRS-only AUC/R2 and is also a framework/portability archetype. Main remaining limitation: the best model’s endpoint is pediatric-specific (not generic asthma) and covariates are unknown, so while evidence is strong, it is not unequivocally superior for all asthma definitions/populations.

All 6 candidates are direct matches at the EFO level (atopic eczema), but endpoint fidelity differs materially. PGS002755 is best supported because its reported phenotype is a generic, target-aligned endpoint (“Incident atopic dermatitis”), uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS; 1,090,702 variants), and reports a PRS effect size (HR high vs low PRS = 1.249, 95% CI 1.123–1.391) in a large European evaluation sample (n=337,910). The two strongest runners-up are PGS004587 (also “Incident atopic dermatitis” with an HR high vs low PRS = 1.153, 95% CI 1.037–1.282; EUR eval; but only 23 genome-wide significant SNPs, which is structurally weaker for a polygenic trait) and PGS001773 (moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis; 25 variants; reports very high full-model AUROC=0.93 and R²=0.49, but these are full-model metrics with multiple demographic/ethnicity covariates and no PGS-only metrics, making the apparent performance hard to interpret and potentially covariate-driven). Confidence is moderate (not high) because none of the candidates report clearly PRS-only AUROC/R², several are therapy-specific paradoxical-eczema endpoints in psoriasis patients (PGS003459/PGS003486/PGS004903) which are less faithful to generic atopic eczema risk, and the best-vs-runner-up comparison relies on effect sizes and structural/method signals rather than directly comparable PRS-only discrimination metrics.

All ranked models are direct matches to atrial fibrillation by trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported. PGS005168 is best supported because it comes from a disease-focused large AF meta-analysis publication ("Meta-analysis of genome-wide associations and polygenic risk prediction for atrial fibrillation in more than 180,000 cases."), reports strong discrimination in its selected European validation record (C-index 0.8718 with CI) and a strong per-SD effect size signal (HR 1.6663), and uses covariates that are largely demographic/technical plus a named clinical risk calculator term (CHARGE-AF). The main limitation is that the inclusion of CHARGE-AF in covariates is a domain-knowledge warning signal for risk-wrapper packaging, so the very high full-model C-index may be partly covariate-driven and not directly comparable as PRS-only performance.

Runner-up PGS005313 is also disease-focused (Nat Commun; cross-population GWAS) with strong reported AUROC (0.78 with tight CI) and strong OR (1.82), and uses relatively light covariates (age, sex). It ranks below PGS005168 because it has less extensive visible performance-record support (record_count 1 vs 45) and its evaluation ancestry field is broad/heterogeneous in the selected record, making direct comparability less clear from the provided metadata.

Second runner-up PGS000016 is a classic disease PRS (Nat Genet 2019; LDpred; genome-wide) with explicit PRS-comparable variance explained (PGS-only R2/Nagelkerke R2 0.029) that is plausibly below the provided EUR heritability ceiling (h2_obs 0.0204; liability 0.0642), and it has large validation size (n=288,978). It ranks behind the two newer disease-focused AF studies because its reported PRS-only signal is modest and its headline AUROC (0.77) is a full-model metric with covariates, which domain guidance says should not be substituted for PRS-only discrimination. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All 4 candidates are direct-match for the target trait (atrial flutter) via trait_reported/trait_efo, but only PGS001263 is specifically labeled and phenotyped as “Atrial flutter” (vs the others’ combined “atrial fibrillation and flutter” endpoints, including one time-to-event formulation). PGS001263 also reports PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.61716; PGS R2=0.02517) plus incremental AUROC, enabling more interpretable PRS contribution than the portability-framework models (PGS001841/PGS002050) that only report partial correlation and lack PRS-only AUROC/R2. However, confidence is limited because PGS001263 (and PGS001339) come from a known pan-trait sparse UKB framework paper (“across 813 traits”), which domain guidance flags as tending to generalize poorly; additionally, its very high listed full-model AUROC (0.78179) is not treated as PRS-only evidence and appears largely covariate-driven given the modest incremental AUROC and PGS-only metrics. Runner-up PGS001339 remains close due to containing flutter in the endpoint and having similar PRS-only metrics, but is penalized for the broader AF+flutter composite and time-to-event phenotyping. Between the two portability-framework options, PGS002050 is preferred over PGS001841 because it has slightly stronger reported partial-r (0.1034 vs 0.1026) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) with far more variants, though both lack PRS-only AUROC/R2 in the visible metadata.

Two direct-match candidates are present (both map to autism spectrum disorder). PGS000327 is best supported because its endpoint fidelity is coherent across fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all explicitly autism spectrum disorder), it comes from an ASD-focused GWAS publication, and it provides supportive PRS-relevant evidence including an OR per SD of 1.33 (moderate) plus an R²-like metric (full_model_r2=0.0245) with only basic covariates (genetic PCs, genotyping wave). PGS002790 is a weaker direct-match runner-up because its phenotyping_reported is explicitly not ASD ("Psychiatric behavior (withdrawn)"), suggesting endpoint mismatch/metadata incoherence despite trait_reported/trait_efo being ASD; its reported partial R² is smaller (0.00546) and it lacks effect-size evidence. Overall outcome is DIRECT_SUB_OPTIMAL (not high-quality) because the best model still lacks clearly PRS-only performance metrics (AUC/PGS-only R² are null) and the only alternative has a notable phenotype-field mismatch, limiting certainty.

All 20 visible candidates are direct matches to basal cell carcinoma by trait_efo, with most also having phenotyping_reported explicitly as “Basal cell carcinoma”; the main endpoint exception is PGS005207 (childhood cancer survivors) and the Nat Commun 2023 models (PGS003416/PGS003417) whose phenotyping_reported is broader (“Keratinocyte cancers”). Among the endpoint-faithful cluster from the same disease-focused PRSweb/Cancer PRSweb family (MGI; basic covariates age/sex/batch/PCs), PGS000452 has the strongest visible performance evidence: highest full-model AUROC (0.632, tied) plus the highest reported Nagelkerke pseudo-R² (0.0487) and a strong per-SD OR (1.663), with a strong top-1% vs rest OR (3.61). Runners-up are near-clones with essentially identical endpoint/covariates and very similar metrics: PGS000454 (AUROC 0.632; pseudo-R² 0.0489; OR 1.661; top-1% OR 3.79) and PGS000456 (AUROC 0.63; pseudo-R² 0.0456; OR 1.633; top-1% OR 3.95). Confidence is Moderate because the key discrimination metric shown is full-model AUROC (PGS-only AUROC/R² are not provided), and several sibling models are extremely close in reported performance, making the top choice sensitive to small, potentially non-comparable metric differences. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All three candidates are direct matches to the target trait (trait_efo includes/equals “bilirubin metabolism disease”). PGS001824 is preferred because its endpoint (“Disorders of bilirubin excretion”) is the most specifically aligned to the target disease concept without being a broader composite (PGS000924 includes porphyrin disorders and is time-to-event), and it comes from the same UKB portability paper as PGS002032 with identical reported partial-r performance (partial-r=0.0716 in EUR), making endpoint fidelity the main differentiator. Between the two bilirubin-excretion siblings, PGS001824 is penalized-regression with 22 variants versus PGS002032’s LDpred2 genome-wide score; however, the visible evidence provides no PRS-comparable AUC/R² for either and shows identical partial-r, so the method/variant-count advantage for PGS002032 is only a structural tie-break rather than decisive—hence moderate confidence. PGS000924 is ranked third despite reporting strong-looking AUROC/R², because it is from a pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with a very small variant set (5) and a time-to-event composite phenotype, which domain guidance flags as less reliable for external performance and endpoint fidelity compared with a direct disease endpoint. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All three candidates are direct matches to the target trait family (bipolar disorder) via trait_reported/trait_efo (bipolar disorder; bipolar I; bipolar II) and share the same publication, method (SDPR), ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/EVAL), and broadly similar variant counts (~935k–949k), so they form a coherent direct-match cluster. However, endpoint fidelity is unclear/possibly mismatched because phenotyping_reported fields are non-diagnostic behavioral/cognitive measures (e.g., cognitive function; DSM5 depression behavior; sluggish cognitive tempo) rather than bipolar disorder case/control status, and the only reported metric is a small full_model_r2/partial R² (no PRS-only AUC/R²), limiting comparability and making ranking weakly supported. Given the target is broad ‘bipolar disorder’, PGS002786 is preferred as the most concept-aligned (bipolar disorder rather than subtype) with otherwise similar evidence; runners-up are the subtype-specific scores PGS002787 (bipolar I) and PGS002788 (bipolar II), with no strong differentiator between them beyond subtype label.

All three candidates are direct matches at the EFO level to the target concept (blood coagulation disease), but they differ in endpoint fidelity and evidence quality. PGS002034 and PGS001826 target a specific congenital coagulation-factor deficiency endpoint (phenotyping_reported matches trait_reported) and come from the same UKB portability framework paper; between these near-clones, PGS002034 is structurally stronger due to a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) with far higher variant count (32,552 vs 45) and essentially identical reported partial-r performance (0.0563 vs 0.0562) under similar ancestry/covariate context, making it the best-supported choice within the visible set. PGS001826 is the closest runner-up because it shares the same endpoint and nearly identical performance evidence but uses a weaker/sparser penalized regression with far fewer variants. PGS001033 is ranked third despite having explicit AUROC/R2 fields because its endpoint is broader/less specific and time-to-event (“TTE other coagulation defects”) and it comes from a pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”), which domain guidance flags as a generalization-risk pattern; additionally it is extremely sparse (1 variant), limiting confidence that it captures polygenic signal. Overall confidence is only moderate because the top two candidates lack PRS-comparable AUROC/R2 (only partial-r is provided) and both are from a portability/framework context rather than a clearly disease-focused multi-cohort coagulation-disorder study. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All shortlisted candidates are direct matches to the target trait (trait_efo=breast carcinoma; phenotyping_reported is breast cancer/incident breast cancer). Among the visible set, PGS004153 (UKBB-EUR.MultiPRS.CV) has the strongest reported discrimination in a like-for-like setting within the same publication family (Am J Hum Genet 2023-12-19; covariates=0; same evaluation ancestry mix EUR/SAS), with full_model_auc=0.6625 and R²=0.0764 plus strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.83, Beta=0.602). The two best-supported runners-up from the same family are PGS004040 (LDpred2.CV; full_model_auc=0.6598; R²=0.0739; OR=1.81) and PGS004025 (LDpred2-auto; full_model_auc=0.6598; R²=0.0736; OR=1.81), which are very close but slightly lower on the reported AUROC/R². Main limitation: these are full-model metrics (not explicitly PGS-only AUROC/R²), and multiple strong direct-match models exist with broadly similar endpoints and evaluation context, so the margin over the top alternatives is modest.

All listed candidates are direct matches to the target trait (celiac disease) via trait_efo and largely aligned phenotyping_reported. PGS000316 is best supported because it targets a straightforward coeliac disease endpoint and reports strong discrimination (full-model AUROC 0.879 with CI 0.87–0.888) with very large validation (n=379,767), providing comparatively robust visible performance evidence among the disease-focused options. Key limitation: the reported AUROC is a full-model metric (no explicit PGS-only AUROC/R²), and covariates are listed as Unknown, so the PRS-only contribution and comparability cannot be confirmed from the provided metadata, lowering certainty.

Runners-up: PGS000040 is a disease-focused celiac prediction model with the highest reported AUROC in the list (0.90), but it is also full-model only with unknown covariates and has a much smaller validation sample (n=2,476). PGS001301 provides explicit PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.82867; PGS R² 0.14224) and uses standard covariates, but it comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank framework paper and has a broader/less specific phenotype label (“Malabsorption/coeliac disease”), which domain guidance treats as a systematic weakness versus disease-focused models when direct disease-focused candidates exist. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All 6 candidates are direct matches (trait_efo=cervical carcinoma; phenotyping_reported is cervical cancer/incident cervical cancer). PGS003428 is best supported overall because it comes from a cervical-phenotype-focused GWAS meta-analysis context and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred; ~2.9M variants), which is structurally favored for polygenic traits versus sparse/GWAS-hit-only scores, and it reports a moderate per-SD HR (1.33). Main limitation: only full-model discrimination is shown (C-index 0.613) with no PGS-only AUROC/R², so comparative performance evidence is incomplete.

Runner-up PGS000073: endpoint is incident cervical cancer with large EUR evaluation and reports HR 1.22 plus C-index ~0.75, but it is a 10-variant genome-wide-significant score from a cross-cancer evaluation paper and the reported AUROC/C-index are full-model metrics with multiple epidemiologic covariates, limiting PRS-only comparability.

Runner-up PGS005165: direct endpoint in an East Asian (EAS) cohort with HR 1.2 and C-index 0.566; it provides non-EUR ancestry coverage absent from most others, but it is also a small GWAS-hit set (15 variants) and has weaker reported discrimination than the leading candidate, with no PRS-only metrics.

All 6 candidates are direct matches to cholelithiasis by trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, with two also using the ICD10 K80 endpoint. However, most candidates lack PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC/R²), making ranking evidence-limited.

PGS005150 is preferred because it is a direct cholelithiasis endpoint (phenotyping_reported: Cholelithiasis) and uses a modern genome-wide shrinkage/transfer method (PRS-CSx) with large genome-wide variant count (908,465) and a non-EUR-specific evaluation context (EVAL: EAS 100%), which is supportive transportability evidence relative to the UKB-only framework/portability scores. Its limitation is that it reports only an effect size (β) without AUROC/R², and training sample size is listed as N/A.

Runners-up: PGS004546 and PGS004476 are both exact ICD10 K80 cholelithiasis endpoints with very large variant counts (1,059,939) and report per-SD ORs (1.2986 and 1.2194, respectively), providing some PRS-signal evidence despite missing AUROC/R² and having unknown covariates. They are ranked ahead of the UKB framework/portability models (PGS001174/PGS001861/PGS002072) because those are explicitly from pan-trait/portability study archetypes per publication titles, and their reported metrics are either missing (PGS001861/PGS002072) or come from a time-to-event framework score (PGS001174), which domain guidance flags as less reliable for external performance despite having PRS-only AUROC/R² available. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All 22 visible candidates are direct EFO matches to chronic kidney disease, but they vary in endpoint fidelity and how interpretable their reported performance is as PRS-specific. PGS002237 is best supported because it is explicitly disease-focused for CKD prediction across ancestries (Nat Med 2022), uses a clear clinically anchored CKD definition (stage 3+; eGFR <45), has large development (n=279,819), multi-ancestry evaluation, and reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.47, 95% CI 1.32–1.65). Although it reports only a full-model AUROC (0.78) with many clinical covariates (so AUROC is not PRS-comparable), the endpoint fidelity plus effect-size evidence and disease-focused study archetype make it the most defensible direct-match choice from the provided metadata.

Runner-up PGS005113 is also a strong direct CKD model with a large-variant PRS-CS construction and a moderate-to-strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.35, 95% CI 1.29–1.41) with basic demographic/PC-style covariates; however, it lacks explicit PRS-only metrics and is framed in a proteomic-marker context, making its comparative evidence slightly less clean than the Nat Med CKD-focused score. Runner-up PGS005090 is compelling for African-ancestry CKD (stage 3+) with very strong reported full-model metrics (AUROC 0.9; R² 0.1) and OR=1.41, but it is ancestry-specific (AFR-only GWAS/EVAL), so it is ranked behind more broadly evaluated CKD scores given no deployment ancestry is specified.

Main limitation lowering confidence: across the pool, PRS-only (no-covariate) discrimination metrics are largely absent (except the pan-trait snpnet model PGS001272, which is endpoint-mismatched/time-to-event and framework-derived), so ranking relies heavily on endpoint fidelity, study archetype, and per-SD OR/HR rather than directly comparable PRS-only AUC/R².

All 10 candidates are direct matches at the EFO level (COPD) but differ in endpoint fidelity and evidence quality. PGS001783 is selected as best supported because it is explicitly COPD in both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported, uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) with very large variant count (884,139), and reports a PRS-comparable metric (Nagelkerke R2 with covariates regressed out = 0.038092) plus an AUROC value (0.74, though not explicitly PRS-only). Its PRS-comparable R2 is consistent with the provided heritability ceiling guidance (h2_liability≈0.0388), supporting metric plausibility. Main limitation: it comes from a global biobank framework-style paper and has relatively small listed validation sample size (n=7,128), and the AUROC appears to be full-model rather than PRS-only.

Runners-up: PGS004536 (J44 COPD) has strong endpoint alignment (ICD J44) and reports a moderate-to-strong per-SD OR (1.4876), but lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and has unknown covariates, lowering comparability. PGS001788 is the closest sibling alternative to PGS001783 (same paper, same method family, COPD endpoint) with much larger validation (n=337,168) but materially weaker PRS-comparable R2 (0.0163) and slightly lower AUROC (0.715), so it ranks behind. Runners-up: PGS000076 and PGS000787 are the next best-supported because they are coherent, endpoint-faithful incident kidney cancer models for renal cell carcinoma with large European validation (n=391,610) and consistent HR per SD (~1.15–1.16) plus similar full-model AUROC (~0.722) and C-index (~0.723–0.724). They rank ahead of other direct matches (e.g., PGS000605/PGS000606 with much lower AUROC 0.517; PGS000722 AUROC 0.567; PGS004690 AUROC 0.5644; PGS003744 has OR 1.24 but very small validation n=692; PGS004245 has HR 1.22 but lacks comparable discrimination metrics).

Direct-match candidates for the target trait (kidney failure) are present, most notably PGS004492 (trait_efo: kidney failure; phenotyping_reported: N18 chronic renal failure) and PGS000708 (trait_reported/efo: Kidney failure, but phenotyping_reported specifies diabetic kidney failure). PGS004492 is preferred because its endpoint label/phenotyping is the most directly aligned to generic kidney failure without an explicit subtype restriction, whereas PGS000708 is explicitly restricted to diabetic kidney failure. However, the evidence is limited because PGS004492 reports no PRS-comparable discrimination metrics (no PGS-only AUC/R²; no full-model AUC) and has unknown covariates, lowering certainty about standalone PRS performance. As runners-up, PGS004562 is similarly well-aligned (kidney failure; N18 chronic renal failure) and shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.39548 vs 1.1708 for PGS004492) but shares the same limitations (no AUC/R²; unknown covariates). PGS000708 is included as the next best-supported alternative due to explicit kidney failure labeling and a reported C-index/full-model metric (0.779) with basic covariates, but its diabetic-only endpoint is a meaningful phenotype mismatch for generic kidney failure. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All 7 candidates are direct matches to the target concept (knee osteoarthritis / gonarthrosis of knee), but the pool has limited PRS-comparable performance reporting (most lack PGS-only AUROC/R²), making the best choice somewhat uncertain.

Best: PGS002729 is the most directly aligned to the target label (“Knee osteoarthritis”; phenotyping_reported: “Clinical osteoarthritis”) and comes from a disease-focused OA PRS paper with multi-cohort development listed. It also reports an AUROC (0.66) with disclosed covariates (age, sex, BMI), which is at least interpretable as a full-model metric (not substituted as PRS-only), providing some comparative evidence.

Runner-up 1: PGS002767 matches the same trait and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with very large variant count, and it reports an OR per SD of 1.35 (moderate discriminative signal) in a sizeable EUR evaluation. However, it lacks AUROC/R², so comparability is limited.

Runner-up 2: PGS004549 is also a direct gonarthrosis/knee OA endpoint (M17) and uses an explicit meta/ensemble-style method name (RFDiseasemetaPRS), which domain guidance treats as a positive structural signal; it reports OR≈1.37. But covariates are unknown and there are no PRS-comparable metrics, lowering confidence.

Not selected as best: PGS001192 is from a pan-trait UKB framework paper (“across 813 traits”) with time-to-event phenotyping; despite having explicit PGS-only metrics, domain guidance warns these sparse framework scores often generalize poorly versus disease-focused alternatives. PGS002749 is a knee replacement endpoint (treatment proxy) with small evaluation and weaker OR (1.13). PGS004479 is a sibling of PGS004549 with slightly lower OR and similarly missing metric/covariate detail. PGS004883 is incident knee OA but appears packaged for incidence estimation with very small training n=404 and only a full-model C-index, making it less supported here.

All 5 candidates are direct matches on concept (trait_efo = late-onset Alzheimer's disease). The strongest PRS-comparable evidence among the set is from the Neurology study siblings PGS000053/PGS000054: both have clear disease endpoint alignment (familial late-onset AD), basic covariates (age, sex), and report per-SD effect sizes; PGS000054 shows a stronger OR=1.73 (vs 1.29 for PGS000053), which domain guidance treats as stronger discriminative signal when AUC/R2 are missing. As runners-up, PGS000053 remains well-aligned and from the same coherent study family but with weaker OR. PGS000334 is also endpoint-aligned and reports an R²=0.191, but this is presented as a generic/full-model variance explained (not explicitly PRS-only) and is unusually high for a simple C+T score with unknown covariates, making comparability/sanity uncertain per the provided domain guidance. Overall confidence is limited because none of the candidates report explicit PRS-only AUROC/R², covariates are unknown for several models, and one candidate (PGS002289) has a phenotyping_reported field that appears to target a cognition-by-age interaction rather than AD diagnosis despite the trait label, reducing endpoint-fidelity clarity.

Direct-match candidates for lung cancer are present (multiple models with trait_reported/phenotyping_reported as lung cancer or closely synonymous endpoints). PGS000078 is best supported in the visible set because it has strong endpoint alignment (incident lung cancer), large European evaluation (n=392,539), and includes effect-size evidence (HR=1.16) alongside high reported discrimination (full-model AUROC=0.846; C-index=0.849). The main limitation is that the reported AUROC/C-index are full-model metrics with extensive covariates (including family history, PM2.5, and detailed smoking terms), and no explicit PRS-only AUROC/R2 is provided, so PRS-specific performance is uncertain. Runners-up: PGS000789 is essentially the same lung-cancer PRS signal (109 variants derived from PGS000078) with the same endpoint/covariate structure and similar metrics (AUROC=0.846; HR=1.17), but it is a derivative/inverse-weight variant rather than the primary construction. PGS004860 has a directly aligned incident lung cancer endpoint and reports very high full-model AUROC (0.893) with basic covariates, but it has much smaller validation (n=24,012) and still lacks PRS-only metrics, making its apparent advantage potentially non-comparable across studies. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

Direct-match candidates are present (multiple SLE/lupus erythematosus models), but most report only full-model AUROC or non-PRS-comparable metrics and several have endpoint restrictions/packaging, so the overall direct-match choice remains somewhat uncertain.

Best pick: PGS000328 is a direct match to lupus erythematosus via systemic lupus erythematosus (trait_reported/trait_efo) and has a clear disease-focused endpoint (SLE, early onset <20) with the strongest reported full-model AUROC among the cleaner SLE-diagnosis-style candidates (AUROC=0.83; EUR eval; n=1,001). While the endpoint is restricted to early-onset SLE (a limitation for generic lupus erythematosus), it avoids explicit phenotype-risk-score packaging and has straightforward GWAS-hit construction.

Runner-up 1: PGS000754 is also a direct SLE model with a genome-wide shrinkage method (lassosum) and very large variant count (293,684), which is structurally favorable for a polygenic disease; it has multi-ancestry evaluation composition and a large validation sample (n=7,733). Its reported full-model AUROC is lower (0.65) and the selected validation ancestry is European despite EAS GWAS, but it remains a strong alternative on method/coverage grounds.

Runner-up 2: PGS000196 is a direct SLE diagnosis endpoint in a clinically relevant setting (rheumatology outpatients with inflammatory arthritis) with moderate full-model AUROC (0.79; EUR eval; n=245). It is penalized relative to the above due to smaller validation size and a more context-specific ascertainment (arthritis clinic), but still aligns well to SLE diagnosis.

Not selected despite high AUROC: PGS003960 reports very high full-model AUROC (0.89) but explicitly uses a 'phenotype risk score' covariate, which domain guidance flags as severe comparability leakage; thus its AUROC is not reliable evidence of PRS quality for direct-match ranking. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

Direct-match candidates are present for the target trait (lymphoid/lymphocytic leukemia). PGS000077 is the best-supported direct match because its trait_efo is exactly lymphoid leukemia and its phenotyping_reported is a direct endpoint (“Incident Lymphocytic Leukemia”), with large European evaluation (n=391,338) and supportive effect size evidence (HR=1.45, 95% CI 1.31–1.61) under basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs). However, the evidence is limited by the fact that only full-model discrimination is reported (AUROC/C-index), with no explicit PRS-only AUROC/R2, so the reported AUROC cannot be treated as purely PRS-comparable.

Runners-up: PGS000788 is also a direct match (lymphocytic leukemia; incident endpoint; same large EUR evaluation n=391,338) and shows a stronger per-SD HR (1.7), but its method explicitly uses inverse weights from PGS000077, creating ambiguity about whether it is a robust improvement versus a reparameterization; it also reports only full-model metrics. PGS000645 is an exact lymphoid leukemia label with PRSweb evaluation and reports an OR per SD (1.358) plus AUROC with CI, but it is based on only 6 variants and has much smaller validation (n=957) with modest discrimination (AUROC 0.578), making it less supported overall than the large-cohort incident-endpoint models.

All 7 listed candidates are direct matches to the target concept (macular degeneration / age-related macular degeneration), but they differ in endpoint fidelity and strength/comparability of performance evidence. PGS004606 is best supported because it has clean phenotype alignment (phenotyping_reported: "Age-related macular degeneration"), comes from a disease-focused AMD genetics study (Nat Genet 2024), uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS; ~1.0M variants), and reports a full-model AUROC of 0.71 with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), plus a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.76, 95% CI 1.73–1.78), which is supportive of meaningful PRS discrimination. Runner-up PGS004607 is from the same study family and method with the same endpoint/covariates, but shows weaker reported performance/effect size (AUROC 0.65; OR 1.48). Third, PGS004952 reports a much higher AUROC, but the metric appears internally inconsistent in the provided metadata (classification_metrics AUROC shown as 84.2 rather than ~0.842) and it targets a narrower endpoint ("Late" AMD) with a small validation sample (n=1,232), making its apparent advantage less reliable from the visible evidence. The main limitation is that several candidates lack PRS-only (no-covariate) discrimination metrics, so comparisons rely on full-model AUROC/effect sizes and study/endpoint coherence rather than directly comparable PGS-only AUC/R² across all models.

Direct-match candidates for melanoma are present (multiple models with trait_efo=melanoma / cutaneous melanoma and melanoma endpoints). PGS000766 is best supported overall because it has strong endpoint fidelity (incident cutaneous melanoma), is disease-focused with broad multi-cohort development (many melanoma-relevant cohorts listed), and reports a moderate per-SD effect size (HR=1.46, 95% CI 1.20–1.77) with a concordance statistic (C-index=0.643). The two strongest runners-up are PGS002247 and PGS002246, which also have high endpoint fidelity (incident invasive melanoma) and provide comparable discrimination evidence (full-model AUROC ~0.691 and ~0.688, respectively) plus reported variance explained (R² ~0.072 and ~0.07). Confidence is Moderate rather than High because many candidates report only full-model AUROC (often with differing covariate sets), PRS-only metrics are generally absent, and there is meaningful competition from other direct melanoma models (e.g., PGS000743/PGS000813 with higher full-model AUROC but smaller/selected validation contexts and/or potentially less generalizable endpoints such as familial melanoma). | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All 6 listed candidates are concept-level direct matches to multiple myeloma via trait_reported/trait_efo (plasma cell myeloma), but endpoint fidelity is inconsistent: PGS003450 has phenotyping_reported="Chronic lymphocytic leukemia" (explicit mismatch), so it is deprioritized despite the myeloma trait fields. Among the remaining coherent myeloma-endpoint models, PGS002281 is best supported by having explicit myeloma phenotyping_reported, European evaluation, and the strongest reported discrimination in the pool with full_model AUROC=0.644 (95% CI 0.622–0.666) plus a strong quintile contrast OR=3.18 (2.34–4.33). However, this is still sub-optimal because none of the candidates report PRS-only AUROC/R2 (the available AUROCs are full-model), and several models are near-ties with similar endpoint alignment and sparse SNP sets. As runners-up, PGS002306 reports the highest full_model AUROC (0.69) but on a much smaller validation sample (n=290) and with unknown covariates, reducing comparability; PGS000653 is next best supported with coherent myeloma phenotyping, basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/batch), larger validation (n=2,738), and moderate per-SD OR=1.327 (1.165–1.511) alongside full_model AUROC=0.577.

All 7 visible candidates are direct matches to the target trait (multiple sclerosis) by trait_efo and phenotyping_reported, so a direct-match exists. PGS002726 is best supported because it is disease-focused (IMSGC), endpoint-aligned (Multiple sclerosis), EUR GWAS/EVAL, and shows the strongest reported discrimination among the set via a European AUROC=0.80 (though this is a full-model metric and covariates are listed as Unknown, limiting PRS-only interpretability). Runner-up PGS000809 is also disease-focused/multi-cohort (many MS cohorts including IMSGC/WTCCC), endpoint-aligned, EUR GWAS/EVAL, and reports full-model AUROC=0.765 plus R²=0.069 and an effect size (β=0.63), giving a richer evidence package than most others. Third, PGS002038 is a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) with very large variant count and a portability-focused publication; it lacks AUROC/R² but has a modest partial-r=0.0396 in European evaluation, making it a plausible alternative. Overall confidence is moderated because several candidates report only full-model metrics (not PGS-only), some have unknown covariates, and two candidates (PGS001270/PGS001271) come from a pan-trait UKB framework despite having explicit PGS-only metrics, creating unresolved comparability/transportability tradeoffs from the visible metadata alone. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

Direct-match candidates are present with exact trait alignment to myocardial infarction (multiple models with trait_efo/phenotyping_reported = myocardial infarction, including PheCode 411.2 and acute MI/I21). Among these, PGS005039 is best supported by (i) direct endpoint fidelity (Myocardial infarction; PheCode 411.2), (ii) genome-wide shrinkage method (ldpred) with very large variant count (1,286,612), and (iii) the strongest visible effect-size evidence in this list (OR=1.578 per SD, 95% CI 1.50–1.67) alongside a competitive C-index (0.7848). Runners-up were chosen from the same MVP MI (PheCode 411.2) family with similarly strong endpoint fidelity and comparable C-index, prioritizing stronger ORs: PGS005035 (OR=1.541; C-index 0.7834) and PGS005045 (OR=1.554; C-index 0.7839). Confidence is Moderate because many near-clone direct MI models have very similar reported discrimination and the reported C-index values are full-model metrics (no explicit PGS-only AUROC/R2 for these MVP models), limiting the ability to cleanly separate top candidates beyond effect-size differences.

Two direct-match candidates are present and both are tightly phenotype-aligned to the target (trait_efo = Nasal Cavity Polyp; phenotyping_reported = ICD10 J33 Nasal polyp) with identical EUR-only development/evaluation context (UKB; DEV/EVAL EUR 100%) and identical variant count (1,059,939), so endpoint fidelity does not differentiate them. Neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (all AUC/R2 fields null), leaving effect size as the main differentiator: PGS004535 reports a stronger per-SD OR (1.600668) than PGS004465 (1.3496), which domain guidance treats as stronger discriminative evidence when AUC/R2 are absent. However, confidence is limited because covariates are unknown for both and the two models come from the same publication family with otherwise near-identical metadata, so the apparent advantage rests largely on a single reported OR without additional corroborating performance metrics.

Both visible candidates are direct matches to the target trait (trait_efo = nicotine dependence; trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = Tobacco use disorder) and come from the same UKB portability publication with similar training (UKB; n=391,124), covariates (sex, age, birth date, deprivation index, 16 PCs), and validation sample size (n=19,400). With endpoint fidelity and study context essentially tied, the main differentiator is the available PRS-comparable performance evidence: PGS002037 shows a higher reported partial correlation (partial-r 0.0741, CI 0.0601–0.0881) than PGS001830 (0.0557, CI 0.0416–0.0697), and it also uses an LDpred2 genome-wide shrinkage approach with substantially more variants (847,691 vs 13,838), which is supportive for polygenic traits when other factors are similar. The overall outcome is still sub-optimal because both models lack standard PRS-only AUROC/R2 (only partial-r is provided) and both originate from a portability-style UKB framework context, limiting confidence about external generalization beyond the reported setting.

All 7 candidates are direct matches to the target concept (nodular goiter) via either benign nodular goiter or nontoxic multinodular goiter; however, the evidence is not cleanly decisive because the strongest-looking models report only full-model AUROC with unknown covariates, and the UKB portability models report only weak partial-correlation metrics.

PGS005262 is best supported among the benign nodular goiter models because it has the most favorable reported discrimination within its near-clone family (full-model AUROC 0.5933 vs 0.5876 for PGS005263 and 0.5854 for PGS005261) while maintaining tight phenotype alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported all point to benign nodular goiter). It also uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRSCS) with very large variant count (~1.09M), which is structurally favorable when endpoint fidelity is comparable.

Runners-up: PGS005263 is the closest sibling (same endpoint, same method family, similar variant count) but with lower AUROC; PGS005261 remains endpoint-aligned but is a sparse P+T score with far fewer variants (110) and the lowest AUROC among the benign-goiter set.

Main limitation lowering confidence: for the PGS00526x/5261 models, covariates are listed as Unknown and the only reported AUROC appears to be full-model (not explicitly PRS-only), so the AUROC differences may not reflect standalone PRS performance. The alternative UKB portability scores (PGS001814/PGS002022) have clean basic covariates but only weak partial-r (~0.024–0.028) and come from a portability framework context, making them less compelling despite clearer covariate reporting.

All 10 listed candidates are direct matches to the target trait (obesity) via trait_efo=obesity and/or obesity-coded endpoints (e.g., ICD10 E66, phecode 278.1). The best-supported choice from the visible evidence is PGS002033 because it has strong phenotype alignment ("Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation"), uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) with very large variant count (846,292), and provides a directly PRS-comparable performance metric (partial correlation 0.0789 in European validation), which is stronger than the analogous sibling PGS001825 (partial-r 0.0547) and more comparable than candidates reporting only full-model R² or only an OR/beta without clear PRS-only metrics. Runners-up: PGS001825 is the closest sibling from the same study with the same endpoint/covariates but weaker partial-r; PGS005235 is endpoint-faithful (obesity phecode 278.1) and uses LDpred2-auto with a large variant count, but lacks PRS-comparable metrics in the provided record, lowering certainty. Overall outcome is DIRECT_SUB_OPTIMAL (not high-quality) because most candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R² and several are from framework/portability-style publications or have endpoint/covariate ambiguities (e.g., time-to-event obesity, BMI as phenotype proxy, unknown covariates), leaving meaningful residual uncertainty despite a preferred pick. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

All 13 candidates are direct matches to the target trait (osteoporosis) by trait_reported/trait_efo, with endpoint fidelity primarily supported by phenotyping_reported (mostly direct osteoporosis diagnosis; some are M81 osteoporosis without pathological fracture or time-to-event). PGS002768 is preferred because it is a direct osteoporosis endpoint and provides an interpretable PRS effect size (OR=1.31, 95% CI 1.25–1.38) with clean/basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical covariates), avoiding reliance on full-model AUROC that may be covariate-driven; several other candidates lack PRS-comparable metrics entirely. Runner-up PGS004565 is also a direct osteoporosis endpoint and reports a slightly stronger per-SD OR (1.328222) but has unknown covariates (comparability uncertainty) and comes from an integration/metaPRS paper where the PRS construction context is less transparent in the visible metadata. Runner-up PGS001273 is a direct osteoporosis endpoint with explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.5685; PGS R2 0.00688) and basic covariates, but it is from a pan-trait sparse UKB framework ("across 813 traits"), which domain guidance flags as tending to generalize poorly; its high full-model AUROC is not treated as PRS-only evidence. Overall confidence is Moderate because the pool mixes framework scores, portability scores with only partial-r, and newer models with missing/unclear PRS-only metrics, making the best choice dependent on limited comparable performance evidence.

Two direct-match candidates are present (both map to trait_efo=otosclerosis). PGS002046 is preferred because its endpoint is a straightforward otosclerosis phenotype (phenotyping_reported: "Otosclerosis") and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very large variant count (570,308), which is structurally favorable for polygenic traits versus sparse selection. However, its reported performance is limited to partial correlation (partial-r=0.0182 in EUR) with no PRS-comparable AUROC/R² provided, which materially limits confidence. PGS001255 is a close runner-up with explicit PRS-only AUROC (0.6319) and PRS-only R² (0.01341) plus incremental AUROC reported, but it is from a pan-trait sparse UKB framework paper ("across 813 traits") and uses a sparse snpnet model with only 213 variants and a time-to-event endpoint ("TTE otosclerosis"), both of which are visible warning signals for generalizability and endpoint comparability. With only these two candidates available and each having different key limitations (missing comparable metrics vs framework/sparse/TTE concerns), the overall direct-match selection remains sub-optimal. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

Direct-match candidates are present (multiple ovarian cancer / ovarian carcinoma / ovarian neoplasm models). PGS000082 is best supported overall because it targets incident ovarian cancer (phenotyping_reported) with aligned trait_efo (ovarian carcinoma), is evaluated in Europeans, and has comparatively strong reported discrimination among broadly-defined ovarian cancer endpoints in this list (full-model AUROC ~0.656 / C-index ~0.655) with a very large validation sample (n=211,958). Key limitation: the reported AUROC/C-index are full-model metrics with substantial covariate adjustment (age, family history, reproductive/hormonal factors, BMI interactions), so they are not clean PRS-only performance and reduce comparability; thus confidence is not high. Runner-up PGS000793 is essentially the same endpoint/covariate package as PGS000082 with similar discrimination (AUROC ~0.66; C-index ~0.654) but uses inverse weights from PGS000082, making it slightly less directly supported than the original. Second runner-up PGS003385 has strong reported AUROC (~0.717) with relatively basic covariates (age, PCs) and large validation (n=143,259), but it is for the serous carcinoma subtype rather than the broader ovarian neoplasm target, so endpoint breadth is narrower despite strong metrics. | Borda re-rank promoted runner-up to primary.

Direct-match candidates are present (multiple pancreatic cancer / exocrine pancreatic carcinoma models), so this is a direct-match selection. PGS000083 is best supported because it has strong endpoint alignment (incident pancreatic cancer; trait_efo exocrine pancreatic carcinoma), large European evaluation (n=391,491), and comparatively strong reported discrimination/effect evidence within this candidate set (full-model AUROC 0.745; C-index 0.742; HR 1.49). Runners-up: PGS000794 is essentially the same 22-variant score family with very similar endpoint/covariates and identical AUROC/HR, but it is explicitly described as using inverse variant weights relative to PGS000083, creating ambiguity about whether it is the intended directionally consistent PRS for risk (hence ranked behind). PGS000663 remains a strong direct match with the same 22-variant genome-wide-significant approach and supportive AUROC (0.67) and OR (1.44), but it has much smaller validation (n=956) and a horizon-conditioned phenotype definition (0–10 years follow-up), which is less generic than the incident-disease endpoint. Overall outcome is DIRECT_SUB_OPTIMAL (not high-quality) because across the pool most reported AUCs are full-model (not PGS-only), covariate sets differ and sometimes include family history/clinical factors (risk-wrapper inflation concern), and the top two candidates are near-clones with unresolved direction/definition differences based on the visible metadata.

All 11 candidates are direct matches at the disease-concept level (trait_efo=Parkinson disease), but several are progression/dementia endpoints (PGS000056 cognitive decline, PGS000211 motor decline, PGS000777 Parkinson’s disease dementia) and are therefore less endpoint-faithful for generic Parkinson disease risk than case/control or incident PD endpoints.

PGS000903 is best supported because it targets Parkinson’s disease with a large, disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis publication family (Lancet Neurol), uses a more polygenic construction (C+T with 1,805 variants vs GWAS-hits-only small sets), and is the only model in the list with an explicit PRS-comparable variance metric reported (R²=0.054) plus a strong stratification effect size (OR top vs bottom quartile 6.25). Its reported full-model AUROC (0.692) is not treated as PRS-only, but is directionally consistent with meaningful PRS signal.

Runner-up PGS000902 is from the same Lancet Neurol study family with the same PD endpoint and clean/basic covariates, but is a GWAS-hits score (90 variants) with weaker/less informative performance evidence (only full-model AUROC 0.651; no PRS-comparable R²/OR shown here).

Second runner-up PGS003763 has strong endpoint fidelity (incident Parkinson Disease) and a very large validation sample (n=314,998) with a clear HR (1.72 high vs low tertile), but it is incident-only (a mild mismatch vs generic PD status) and lacks PRS-only metrics; thus it is slightly less supported than the Lancet Neurol family given the available metadata.

Main limitation: across the pool, most candidates report only full-model AUROC or HR/OR without explicit PGS-only AUROC/R², and covariate sets differ (some include family history or other non-genetic predictors), which reduces certainty in cross-model comparability and keeps confidence at Moderate.

All 4 candidates are direct/near-direct matches to the target concept (peripheral vascular disease), but they differ in endpoint fidelity and evidence strength. PGS005217 is preferred because it is a disease-focused PAD score with an explicit incident PAD endpoint, very large multi-cohort validation (n=304,294) across multiple ancestries, uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) with a large variant set (1,296,292), and reports a strong PRS effect size (HR=1.66 per SD; 95% CI 1.61–1.71). The main limitation is that the target is broader than PAD (PVD umbrella), and the only discrimination metric shown is a full-model C-index (0.731) rather than a clearly PRS-only AUC/R2, so PRS-only comparability is incomplete.

Runners-up: PGS002055 and PGS001843 are exact-label matches to peripheral vascular disease (unspecified) but come from a UKB portability framework paper (a negative study-archetype signal per domain knowledge). Between them, PGS002055 ranks above PGS001843 due to slightly stronger reported PRS-comparable evidence (partial-r 0.0175 vs 0.0151) and a much larger variant count (599,514 vs 242), with otherwise similar endpoint/covariates/validation context. PGS005158 is deprioritized because its phenotype is restricted to PAD in type 2 diabetes with heavy clinical/treatment covariates and only a modest HR (1.13), making it less suitable as a general PVD PRS despite being PAD-aligned.

All three candidates are direct-match at the EFO level (trait_efo=preeclampsia), but endpoint fidelity differs. PGS003586 is best supported because it is explicitly reported as Pre-eclampsia and uses a direct hypertensive-disorders-of-pregnancy endpoint (phenotyping_reported: Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia), with basic covariates (maternal age, age^2, PCs) and a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.31, 95% CI 1.24–1.38) in European evaluation. PGS003587 is a close sibling from the same Nat Med study with essentially the same endpoint/covariates but is labeled gestational hypertension and shows a weaker effect size (OR=1.20), so it ranks second. PGS004593 has the exact trait_reported label (Preeclampsia) and large evaluation n, but its phenotyping_reported is gestational hypertension (a partial mismatch for a preeclampsia target) and it reports HR=1.16 (weaker signal), making it the third choice. Overall confidence is limited because none of the candidates provides PRS-comparable AUC/R2 in the visible metrics, so ranking relies mainly on endpoint alignment and effect-size magnitude.

All shortlisted candidates are direct matches for the target trait (prostate cancer / prostate carcinoma) based on trait_reported/trait_efo and generally aligned phenotyping_reported. PGS003415 is best supported because it has strong endpoint fidelity for generic risk deployment ("5 years incident prostate cancer risk"), large external validation (n=170,850), and a strong reported discrimination metric (C-index 0.79 with CI) without explicitly disclosed heavy biomarker covariates (covariates listed as Unknown). The main limitation is that it is explicitly a fixed-horizon (5-year) incident-risk endpoint, which domain guidance flags as risk-wrapper packaging and potentially less comparable to generic disease status PRS; covariates are also not specified.

Runners-up: PGS005238 and PGS004155 are both direct prostate cancer models with large validation (each n=184,010 and n=171,474 respectively) and strong reported full-model AUROC (~0.789 and ~0.705). PGS005238 is preferred over PGS004155 because it targets the same 5-year incident endpoint and reports higher AUROC with similar packaging/covariate framing (age-specific absolute risk adjusted by PGS relative risk).
